rationale: A wins because it finds the sharpest reporter-grade claim in the update and turns it into a real beat: "The installer bottleneck: a home battery that claims it skips the rewiring." B is competent, but it keeps circling the same brand-extension story with "The power-bank company just built a whole-home battery" and "Why a phone-charger giant is betting on home energy storage." A gives the founder four usable doors into coverage; B gives three doors, and two open into the same room.
gaps_in_A: "battery storage is becoming a consumer-electronics product" is a big category claim resting on one launch. A asks for proof, good, but the angle is still carrying more weight than the supplied facts can hold alone.

"What a homeowner is actually buying when they buy backup power" is useful, but A admits it needs "at least one real US household using the system". Without that customer, it is an explainer idea, not a pitch-ready angle.

A underuses the fact that Anker is "large, profitable, publicly traded" as its own investor/business-strategy lane; it folds that proof into the category angle instead of making the capital-allocation question cleaner.
gaps_in_B: "Anker naming Tesla Powerwall as direct competition" is overclaimed. The update says the product competes with Powerwall; it does not say Anker named Tesla or explicitly positioned against it.

"The power-bank company just built a whole-home battery" and "Why a phone-charger giant is betting on home energy storage" are dressed as separate angles, but both are basically the same category-stretch story.
"Story type: contrarian" is wrong. "Anker makes small portable gadgets" versus "Anker launched a home battery" is not a contrarian take; it is the announcement with a hat on.
B buries the best angle in a proof note: "installs without major electrical rewiring" should be its own installer-channel story, not supporting detail for a Tesla comparison.
